items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the environmental conservation law, in relation to establishing a product stewardship program for primary batteries
items.lawCode: Add Art 27 Title 16 §§27-1601 - 27-1627, amd §3-0301, En Con L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S4522

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the environmental conservation law, in
relation to establishing a product stewardship program for primary
batteries

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL: The purpose of the bill is to require
participation in a battery stewardship plan (recycling plan) by
producers of primary batteries or primary battery-containing products.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill amends Article 27 of the environmental
conservation law by adding a new title 16 that will mandate
participation by producers of primary batteries or primary
battery-containing products in a battery stewardship (recycling) plan.

Section 27-1601 sets forth definition for all terms of this new title
including the definition of primary battery which means a
nonrechargeable battery weighing two kilograms or less, including
alkaline, carbon-zinc, lithium-metal, and other batteries typically
generated as waste.

Section 27-1603 states that the beginning January 1, 2017 a producer
of a primary battery or primary batter-containing product shall not
sell, offer for sale, or deliver to a retailer for subsequent sale a
primary battery or primary battery-containing product unless a
producer or stewardship organization is registered under an approved
and implemented primary battery stewardship plan and the name of the
producer and the producer's brand are designated on the department
website as covered by an approved primary battery stewardship plan.

Beginning September 1, 2016, the primary battery stewardship
organization must file a registration Form with the commissioner on a
registration form that includes a list of producers of primary
Batteries and primary battery-containing products of each producer
participation in the Stewardship organization and the name address and
contact information of a person responsible for ensuring the producers
compliance with this chapter. New producers must also comply with this
title within 90 days after supplying notice to the commissioner of its
intent to sell, offer for sale or offer for promotional purposes a
primary battery or primary battery-containing product.

An exemption to the requirements of this title are provided to
producers whose total retail value of sales of covered batteries is
less than $500.

Section 27-1605 requires that on or before April 1, 2016, each
producer of primary batteries shall individually or as part of a
primary battery stewardship organization submit a primary battery
stewardship plan to the commissioner for review. Each stewardship plan
must provide for the free collection of batteries from consumers and a
producer cannot refuse the collection of a primary battery based on
the brand or manufacturer of the primary battery.

The collection provisions require that all retailers that sell covered
batteries under the plan and municipalities to opt to be a collection


facility; to provide no fewer than two collection facilities in each
county of the state; and to provide for the acceptance from a consumer
of up to twenty batteries per visit or more at the facility's
agreement.

The battery stewardship plan must also include provisions for
education and outreach programs including media advertising, retail
displays and other public education efforts which at a minimum notify
the public that there is a free collection program for all primary
batteries and the location of the collection points and how to access
the collection program.

The plan must also include reimbursement procedures for another
primary battery producer or stewardship organization with an approved
plan for the actual direct costs per unit of weight incurred in
collecting the brands or products of the producer submitting the plan.

The plan must include implementation provisions which provide for
implementation of the program at no cost to retailers or
municipalities acting as collection facilities under the program and
the producer must provide the collection facilities with the necessary
equipment for setting up the collection point and for providing the
pickup of collected primary batteries.

Section 27-1607 requires the submission of an annual report beginning
on or before April 1, 2018 and requires a plan audit once every five
years done by an independent third party auditor.

Section 27-1609 sets forth the requirements for a primary battery
stewardship organization which must, in order to qualify as a
stewardship organization, commit to assume the responsibilities,
obligations, and liabilities of all producers participating in the
organization, not create unreasonable barrier for participation by
producers and maintain a public website that lists all producers and
brands covered by the collection plan. The stewardship organization
must register with the commissioner annually beginning on January 1,
2016.

Section 27-1611 requires the commissioner to determine whether the
plan complies with the requirements of Section 27-1605 within 90 days
after receipt of the plan and must publish all proposed and approved
plans on the department's website. The commissioner must also make the
plans available for public review and comment prior to approval of the
plan. The term of the stewardship plan shall be no more than 5 years.

Section 27-1613 imposes obligations on the retailers including the
requirement that no primary battery or primary battery-containing
product unless the retailer has reviewed the department's website to
determine that the producer in implementing an approved collection
plan or is part of a product stewardship organization. The retailer is
also provided with certain exceptions to these requirements with
regard to inventory and in situations where the producer's
registration is expired or revoked after the retailer took possession
of the primary batteries.

Section 27-1615 addresses confidentiality of certain portions of data
that is covered by exemptions to the freedom of information law. This


section also states that total weight of batteries collected is not
confidential business information exempted under the freedom of
information law.

Section 27-1617 sets forth authorized activity not subject to the
state's antitrust, restraint of trade, and unfair trade practice laws
or other trade or commerce regulations to the extent reasonably
necessary to plan, implement and comply with the chosen system for
managing discarded primary batteries. However, this authorized
activity is not applicable to agreements amongst producers, retailers,
wholesalers or stewardship organizations that affect pricing of
primary batteries or primary battery-containing products.

Section 27-1619 sets forth administrative fees to be assessed annually
to producers of stewardship organizations in the amount of $15,000.

Section 27-1621 creates a private right of action for producers of
primary battery stewardship organizations to bring a civil action
against another producer or stewardship organization for damages when
the plaintiff incurs more than $3,000 in actual direct costs
collecting, handling, recycling or disposing of primary batteries sold
or offered for sale by another producer. A private right of action is
also created for a producer or stewardship organization when
reimbursement requests are ignored or payment is not made.

Section 27-1623 sets forth reimbursement provisions, audit requests
and private right of action to bona fide rechargeable battery
stewardship programs for direct costs incurred in the collection of
primary batteries.

Section 27-1625 sets forth a civil penalty of not more than $1,000 per
day for each day of noncompliance with this title.

Section 27-1627 addresses rulemaking authority of the commissioner.

Section 2 of the bill amends subdivision 2 of section 3-0301 of the
environmental conservation law by adding a new paragraph dd giving the
department and the commissioner authority to enforce a product
stewardship program.

Section 3 of the bill sets forth an immediate effective date.

JUSTIFICATION:  In 2010, New York State implemented the "Rechargeable
Battery Law" which recognized that these batteries contained toxic
metals such as cadmium and lead and called for a program of recycling
to prevent exposure to the environment from lead and acid
contamination which could cause serious public health consequences.

It is time for the State to recognize that primary batteries also
contain dangerous and toxic metals which not only create excessive
waste from their disposal but can also create long term and serious
dangers to the environment caused by their improper disposal into
landfills, etc. Although most household batteries no longer contain
dangerous mercury, there are other heavy metal components including
zinc, lead, cadmium, and nickel and manganese which can contaminate
the environment when primary batteries containing these metals are
disposed of improperly. According the United States Environmental


Protection Agency, "when incinerated, certain metals might be released
into the air or can concentrate in the ash produced by the combustion
process." In California and in various countries in Europe, all
batteries are considered hazardous waste when discarded and/or are
required to be separated from regular domestic waste when discarded.

Improper disposal of primary batteries presents an unnecessary impact
on the environment that can be easily addressed by implementing a
primary battery recycling program.

In addition, according to the Corporation for Battery Recycling,
batteries that contain metals such as zinc, steel and manganese can be
recycled for use in other applications and this in turn can "reduce
the mining and refining of zinc, iron and manganese ore" providing yet
another benefit to the environment.

It is time for New York State to join states like Vermont and
Connecticut in implementing mandatory "single use" battery recycling
laws

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY: New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS: None to the state.

EFFECTIVE DATE:  This act shall take effect immediately

B.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S4522B

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the environmental conservation law, in relation to
establishing a product stewardship program for primary batteries

 PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL :

The purpose of this bill is to establish a battery recycling program
for consumers.

 SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS :

This bill would:

*define relevant terms including "primary battery," which would mean a
non rechargeable battery, including alkaline, carbon-zinc, and lithium
metal, weighing two kilograms or less;

*prohibit the sale of primary batteries unless the producer is
registered with the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) and
has an approved battery stewardship plan;

*require battery stewardship plans to include:

o all producers and contact information;
o brands of batteries covered by the plan;
o free collection from consumers;
o method of disposition;
o a description of roles and responsibilities; and,
o education and outreach

*require a producer to submit an annual report to DEC; and,

*establish parameters for DEC involvement to include:

o plan approval;
o website posting of all proposed and approved plans;
o maintenance of producer names and brands on the DEC website; and,
o receipt of producer registration fees.

 JUSTIFICATION :

This legislation would authorize New York to expand its recycling
efforts beyond rechargeable batteries to address other types of
batteries by requiring battery manufacturers to establish a consumer
collection program. Batteries contain metals such as zinc, steel and
manganese that can be recycled, helping to reduce the need for mining
and refining. Several other states including Vermont and Connecticut
have adopted battery recycling programs.

 PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

This is new legislation.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS :

Minimal State fiscal implications.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect 90 days after enactment.
